sentences.text: Aepyornis was an extinct genus of elephant birds that lived only on Madagascar. It was a ratite that could not fly and lacked a keel on its breast bone. Like the cassowary, ostrich, rhea, emu, and kiwi, Aepyornis was a flightless bird with a sternum lacking a keel.
A. maximus weighed between 275 and 1000 kg and reached a height of 3 meters. Aepyornis was the largest bird in the world, reaching 3 meters in height and weighing nearly half a ton, or 400 kilograms.

Both species had small heads with straight, thick conical beaks, though the beak was proportionally larger in A. hildebrandti. The neck of Aepyornis was proportionally long, containing 16 to 17 cervical vertebrae.

The wings of Aepyornis were vestigial. The pelvic bones of Aepyornis were heavily fused, making their individual boundaries difficult to discern. The hindlimbs were proportionally long and robust, with a particularly short and thick femur. The terminal toe bones of Aepyornis were broad and not hooked.
Aepyornis eggs are the largest known for any amniote, with volumes of 5.6 to 13 litres. An Aepyornis egg has about 160 times the volume of a chicken egg.
Archaeological evidence suggests Aepyornis eggs regularly provided meals for entire human families.
Aepyornis eggs have been found with a circumference of up to one meter. Fossilized eggs of Aepyornis have been found with a circumference of over 1 meter and a length of up to 34 centimeters.
A. maximus is commonly known as the "elephant bird," a term possibly originating from Marco Polo's 1298 reference to the mythical roc.
The genus Aepyornis was described by I. Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire in 1851. The genus Aepyornis was named by Geoffroy in 1850.
DNA from Aepyornis eggs was successfully extracted and published in 2010.
The National Geographic Society in Washington possesses an intact Aepyornis egg specimen containing an embryonic skeleton, which was given to Luis Marden in 1967.
BBC presenter David Attenborough owns an almost complete fossilized eggshell of Aepyornis that he assembled from fragments collected during a visit to Madagascar.

Brain endocasts show that Aepyornis had greatly reduced optic lobes, consistent with a nocturnal lifestyle. Larger olfactory bulbs in A. maximus suggest it occupied forested habitats, while A. hildebrandti likely occupied open habitats.
A 2022 isotope study suggested A. hildebrandti was a mixed feeder with a large grazing component, while A. maximus was probably a browser.
An intact embryonic skeleton of Aepyornis was found in an egg that was 80-90% of the way through incubation.
Possible remnants of medullary bone used for egg calcium have been found in the femurs of A. maximus.
The closest living relative of Aepyornis is the New Zealand kiwi. DNA comparisons suggest elephant birds diverged from New Zealand kiwis over 50 million years ago.

Some authors consider that up to four species existed within the genus Aepyornis, including Aepyornis hildebrandti, Aepyornis gracilis, Aepyornis medius, and Aepyornis maximus. However, later studies recognize only one or two species within the genus: Aepyornis maximus and Aepyornis hildebrandti.
Aepyornis belongs to the family Aepyornithidae.
The genus Aepyornis became extinct around 1000 AD.
Aepyornis lived from the Late Pleistocene to the Holocene, between 0.129 and 0 million years ago.
Later DNA studies suggest Vorombe titan is indistinguishable from A. maximus and likely represents large females of that species.
It is debated whether Aepyornis extinction was a secondary effect of diseases transferred from domesticated fowl.
